claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The initial catalyst uses a low or minimal amount of platinum-group metal.
Thermal treatment in an NH3-containing atmosphere can introduce nitrogen into the alloy lattice.
Nitrogen doping will form multiple robust metal-nitrogen bonds in the catalyst.
The modification will produce a surface layer partially enriched in platinum-group elements.
Nitrogen incorporation and metal-nitrogen bonding induce lattice distortion in the alloy core.
Metal-nitrogen bonds stabilize the alloy structure and enhance corrosion resistance and durability.
Nitrogen incorporation promotes controlled surface segregation that generates a platinum-group-metal-rich surface.
The modified surface electronic structure improves reactant adsorption and desorption dynamics.
Improved adsorption and desorption dynamics lower activation barriers for exhaust-gas oxidation reactions.
Nitrogen doping will lower CO and hydrocarbon light-off temperatures and enable efficient oxidation below 150 °C.
Nitrogen doping will reduce catalyst poisoning or deactivation caused by H2O and NO.
The nitrogen-doped catalyst will retain activity better than the unmodified catalyst during extended automotive-exhaust aging.
The activity, poisoning-resistance, and durability improvements can be achieved without increasing total platinum-group-metal content.
Excessive or spatially uneven nitrogen doping could block active sites or excessively disrupt the alloy structure.
The benefits require an optimized nitrogen-doping level and may not persist in extreme environments outside typical automotive-exhaust conditions.
